https://www.gdnonline.com:443/Details/14.text: Rescuers work at the site of a Russian missile strikes in Kyiv region yesterday At least 15 people have been killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, including 10 dead in ballistic missile strikes on an exhibition near Kyiv showcasing drone technology. Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said some 100 people had been injured in the daytime attack on the exhibition, attended by prominent members of the defence sector. Elsewhere, five people were killed in the eastern city of Sloviansk by Russian glide bombs. And last night, Zelensky said he had received intelligence that Russia was preparing another massive missile strike which “could happen today” or “within the next 48 hours”. Meanwhile, an overnight Ukrainian strike killed six people and wounded 26 in the Russian city of Kirov, more than 1,000km behind the front line. Ukraine also attacked warehouses of Wildberries – Russia’s biggest online retailer. After the attacks near Kyiv, there were initially fears for the safety of Defence Ministry adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, also known as Flash, and Lyuba Shypovych, who has been involved in developing technology for the Ukrainian army. Following the incident, both took to social media to confirm they were unharmed, and Beskrestnov said he had stayed away from the event because of security concerns. Ukrainian air force spokesman Yuri Ihnat told Ukrainian TV the attack involved three ballistic missiles, only one of which was intercepted. Russia confirmed the attack. Its Defence Ministry said high-precision long-range weaponry had been used on a site where drones for use in targeting civil sites in Russia were being demonstrated. It said producers of drones, as well as representatives of Ukraine’s drone forces and security services “directly planning and carrying out strikes on Russian territory” were present. This is at least the third time since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 that an exhibition of this kind has been hit. There has been widespread outrage that a public event of this kind was being held at all and had, apparently, been widely advertised. Zelensky said the incident was being investigated, while Ukraine’s prosecutor-general said efforts were under way to establish who decided to hold the event and what safety measures were in place. The attack came hours after the Ukrainian strikes on a factory in the city of Kirov and warehouses in north-west Russia. Zelensky said “one of the most important military facilities” in Kirov supplying “components for aircraft and missile equipment” used in strikes against Ukraine had been hit. Yesterday’s attacks on at least two Wildberries facilities in the St Petersburg area were the latest of several over the past week. The attacks on the retailer have dealt a blow to a large number of small and medium-sized businesses within Russia. After months of drone attacks on oil depots and refineries, Kyiv says it is targeting logistics hubs – such as those run by Wildberries – because they can be used to buy military equipment, in order to disrupt supplies to the Russian army. Meanwhile Zelensky is expected to travel to the US next week, and is slated to meet President Donald Trump on Tuesday, a White House official said, as Washington seeks to revive peace talks between Ukraine and Russia. Trump ally Laura Loomer, who is in Kyiv and interviewed Zelensky, quoted him as saying he intends to go to the funeral of US Senator Lindsey Graham. Meanwhile, Romanian President Nicusor Dan said a Romanian F-16 fighter jet shot down a Russian drone breaching the country’s airspace yesterday.

Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images First Edition newsletter Russia Tuesday briefing: Europe thinks Russia is preparing to test Nato’s limits In today’s newsletter: Intelligence chiefs warn that Russia’s appetite for risk is growing, as sabotage and other covert attacks target countries supporting Ukraine Libby Brooks Tue 22 Sep 2026 01.40 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 01.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. As the UN general assembly kicks off in New York later today, we anticipate a heavy focus on the ongoing conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and the Gulf – as well as the inevitable body language analysis of Andy Burnham’s first in-person meeting with Donald Trump. But another related conflict is likely to dominate informal discussions: the intensifying acts of sabotage on European states that are believed to trace back to Russia but deliberately fall below the threshold for military response – a so-called hybrid or “shadow war” with the singular purpose of disrupting support for Ukraine. As Vladimir Putin consolidates his grip on power in tightly controlled Russian elections and the Kremlin welcomed further success for the far-right AfD in German state polls yesterday, European intelligence officers have shared with the Guardian their starkest warnings yet about potential Russian attempts to test Nato resolve with an attack on European soil. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Shaun Walker , our special correspondent for eastern Europe, Ukraine and intelligence matters, about whether Europe is already at war. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories Yemen | The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. Environment | The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months before its expected peak. Gaza | Israeli and UK military commanders could be requested to give evidence to an inquest concerning three British aid workers killed in Gaza when aid vehicles they were travelling in were hit by an airstrike. US | After President Trump’s snap decision to ban CNN from the White House, the four other networks that comprise the White House’s TV pool decided they would cease their pooled coverage of the president. Slavery | Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged. In depth: The line between peace and war View image in fullscreen Locals watch as firefighters work after a Russian drone attack struck a residential building in Kyiv, on 1 September. Photograph: Francisco Seco/AP In a series of interviews with Shaun Walker in Prague and Riga, European intelligence bosses from the Czech Republic, Latvia and Sweden raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one suggesting a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”. These sources were speaking days after Polish prime minister Donald Tusk told his parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months. French president Emmanuel Macron has also summoned party leaders for an emergency meeting to discuss similar warnings. When I catch up with Shaun in a taxi on the way to Warsaw airport, he’s still assessing the gravity of these warnings. “One thing you always have to bear in mind when reporting on intelligence is that – because the way spy agencies gain information usually remains secret – you often don’t know if a source is talking about a very specific intercept of a plan that’s almost certainly going to happen, or if it’s less concrete chatter that analysts have put together.” His view is that these concerns are not at the level of early 2022, when American intelligence repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade Ukraine and had hard evidence of the Kremlin’s plans ( as Shaun revealed here ). What did surprise him was his sources’ willingness to be quoted: “Normally I go into these interviews assuming that we’re going to talk off the record. All of these people were happy to be on the record, which does suggest they want to get a message out.” (Quick note, readers: “off the record” is a phrase that reporters in books, films and even real life throw about with abandon, but what does it mean? Say your source tells you about seeing a piece of fruit in a bowl. On the record means you can report that Jill Bloggs told the Guardian exclusively: “There’s a banana in the fruit bowl.” Off the record allows you to use that information to aid your investigation, but you mustn’t reveal where it came from. You can approach other fruit bowl-watchers, to check if they agree with Jill’s sighting. Then you might write: “Several sources with knowledge of the fruit bowl confirmed that a banana was present.” It’s a journalistic convention with no legal consequences, of course.) What is this hybrid war and how can Europe fight it? View image in fullscreen Lithuanian soldiers secure the area where Italian fighter jets shot down a drone during a Nato mission, 55.9 miles northwest of the capital Vilnius on 15 Sep. Photograph: Mindaugas Kulbis/AP This systematic campaign has developed since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, with common features: designed to seed chaos and anxiety among Ukraine’s allies, while it is often difficult to prove conclusively Russian involvement as Kremlin security services pivot to recruiting local foot soldiers online. Since the beginning of this year, there has been a catalogue of unexplained fires at defence facilities supplying Ukraine in Italy, Bulgaria, Estonia and Slovakia. An explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport. Authorities in Denmark warned Russia is recruiting Danish citizens to sabotage defence firms ​with ties to Ukraine; in Lithuania, an Ikea was set on fire ; and in France, five coffins inscribed with the words “French soldiers in Ukraine” were left under the Eiffel Tower . In the UK, the Rycroft review found online disinformation from hostile foreign states including Russia was warping political discourse when it published in March, while two Russian-linked arsonists who targeted property connected to former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer were jailed in June. Given the recent escalation, it’s not surprising that Shaun observes some EU politicians “getting irritated” with the term ‘hybrid war’, and arguing that such direct attacks amount to more than “grey zone” activity. Although European governments have become much quicker publicly to call out Russian involvement, the challenge for these politicians is deciding what effective measures they can take. After the Leipzig incident, Germany expelled more than 150 Russian diplomats and promised tighter border controls for Russians entering Germany. But the Schengen free movement zone makes this tricky: one of the suspects in the Leipzig incident reportedly entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa. EU sanctions blacklist Russian banks and energy companies, as well as entities in the United Arab Emirates, Thailand and China for helping Moscow evade western restrictions. And there’s a growing willingness among EU nations to clamp down on Russia’s shadow fleet – ships illegally carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas. While there are vocal critics who argue these diplomatic and economic measures don’t go far enough, others worry that even more decisive responses would riskdragging the bloc into military escalation. “What Russia is working to is that they know even the most hawkish people in Nato countries would really like to avoid having a direct conflict.” What is the mood in Europe? For decades, politicians and analysts in those Baltic states most at risk of Russian aggression have warned western Europe to take that threat more seriously. But that mood has flipped of late, with the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, for example, cautioning against “panic” on social media. These states remain the strongest voices in terms of tangible responses to Russian aggression, but are well aware that the vast majority of Russia’s military capability is tied up in Ukraine. They are also concerned about the impact that a narrative of tanks rolling into Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania has on their societies and economies – which is of course partly the point of concerted Russian psyops. “Somebody put it to me recently – which I thought was the perfect description – that Baltic states prefer western Europe to see it as a chronic rather than an acute problem”. With that in mind, European leaders at the UN in New York this week will be keen to create a united front and wary of interventions from Donald Trump, who has previously dismissed concerns that Russia will strike a Baltic country or other member state to test Nato resolve and repeatedly criticised the alliance. Is Europe already at war (and what does that mean)? When Shaun was researching his latest book, The Illegals , about Russia’s deep-cover spies, he waded through archives of KGB documents from the 70s and 80s. They often referred to “the special period”, a Soviet term that described a stage between friendly coexistence and war between communist and capitalist worlds, and was characterised by plans for relentless sabotage. “It sounded a lot like where we are now”, he says. Like Europe, Russia doesn’t want a direct confrontation with the West but it’s clear, adds Shaun, “that their risk appetite is increasing.” The scale of sabotage has led to prominent military voices in the UK and across Europe suggesting that the bloc is already at war – although the very definition of ‘at war’ is now liminal – and that governments ought to be more transparent with their public. Does he agree? Shaun’s one word answer is “no”. The nuance is as follows: “There is a clear campaign from Russia, using methods that are not military, but are pretty aggressive. Some people may consider them as being something close to a war. It’s clearly absolutely nothing like the war in Ukraine.” He suggests that European governments find themselves in a bind domestically. “If they choose to spend on defence rather than social issues, those social issues get worse and voters move to the populist right, the AfD in Germany or Le Pen in France, then you end up with leaders who are very sympathetic to Russia in power.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “There’s a careful path between dismissing this as a fake threat and the kind of alarmist rhetoric that we’re on the path to war and every other issue is secondary.” What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen Alaa Hessi, an eight-month pregnant Palestinian woman, describes her daily routine in a new Guardian series detailing life under occupation in Gaza. Today in Focus: The Latest View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian Rise of the far right in Germany: how worried should we be? The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office despite heavy losses in two state elections that he described as a ‘disaster’. The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland won with 38% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the leftwing Die Linke was victorious in Berlin. Merz has promised political change, but speculation is growing that his party could soon oust him. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Berlin correspondent , Deborah Cole. Photograph: Handout Despite 18 million people in the UK having hearing issues, there is still no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now, Amanprit Arnold, an urban planner and activist, is campaigning to create one . The DeafCity Hub would be a national centre for Arnold’s community, as well as a co-working and cultural space, and a home for Deaf-sector charities. It would be designed using deaf-friendly architectural guidelines called DeafSpace principles, which include wide corridors and staircases so people can walk

https://www.dw.com/en/russia-s-attacks-o.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OaIc Russian attacks have turn Ukraine's capital into a front-line city Image: Marina Asmolowa/DW Advertisement Until a few months ago, life was relatively peaceful in Kyiv when compared with the situation near the war's front lines elsewhere in Ukraine . Now, as Russia expands its attacks on the capital, Kyiv has increasingly become a front-line city. With too few shelters for the 4 million residents of Kyiv , subway stations double as makeshift dormitories. Starting at about 10 every night, people create sleeping areas with mattresses and small tents. Children snuggle up to adults; pets seek comfort from their owners or find a spot among strangers between the cold walls. "We're alive," Halyna told DW, holding her 5-year-old son, Roman, close. "We've been lucky once again." Most evenings — even when no air-raid siren has sounded — she takes the boy to the nearest subway station. Her apartment is located in the Lukyanivka district, which Russia has systematically targeted over the war's four years and eight months. People lie on mattresses in the capital's subway system during the night Image: Marina Asmolowa/DW 'These sick monsters don't care who they kill' In September, 14-year-old Daniel Umanskyj was doing homework in his room when a Russian drone struck the apartment building in the central district of Pechersk. A neighbor named Vlad happened to be in the hallway with his daughter at the time of the strike. "We were late that day — and this saved our lives," Vlad said. "Daniel's death is a tragedy." He added: "These sick monsters don't care who they kill." Flowers have been planted in front of the damaged apartment building in memory of Daniel. Russia also targets places where children gather. In early October, a drone struck a school building in southwestern Kyiv. Fortunately, pupils and teachers were already in shelters at the time. "We've been teaching all the pupils in person because we have a large shelter that can accommodate more than 500 students," Valentyna Chorna, the school's principal, told DW. As there is enough space in the shelter for everyone, students in the first through ninth grades are able to go to school, she said. 14-year-old Daniel was killed when an attack hit his building in Kyiv Image: Marina Asmolowa/DW Danger at home, at school — everywhere Whether classes take place depends not only on the decision of the parents and the school administration: It also depends on whether shelters are available and how long the air-raid siren continues to sound. If an alarm sounds in the morning while children are still at home, they may not be able to go to school that day. "This is an enormous burden for parents," said a colleague from the DW bureau in Kyiv, whose daughter attends school. "You have to go to work — and the child stays home alone." "Even the walk to school is dangerous because an air-raid alarm can go off at any time," she said. Her daughter attends a school not far from the Antonov aircraft factory. "One day she texted me: ‘You can't imagine what a huge explosion that was!'" she said. "I don't know if something was shot down or if there was a strike somewhere." She added: "Things like that really scare children." And staying home brings its own risks. In September, a Russian drone struck their building. The apartment itself wasn't damaged, and her daughter was at school that morning, but it was another reminder of just how much survival has become a matter of luck. When an air-raid siren sounds, no one knows who will be spared, she said. Attacks on Kyiv target civilian infrastructure, schools and places where children spend free time Image: Marina Asmolowa/DW Kyiv's population persists Russia's attacks have become deadlier in 2026. According to the military administration in Kyiv, 140 people were killed in the capital during the first eight months of the year, compared with 172 for all of 2025. If this trend continues, 2026 could become Kyiv's deadliest year since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022. Attacks on warehouses have led to shortages in supermarkets on a scale not seen since the early months of the war. At the end of September, emergency power outages resumed in Kyiv. The subway was paralyzed by a Russian attack. Given the strikes on the energy infrastructure, it is unclear how the capital can reliably supply residents with heat, electricity and water during the upcoming winter. Despite Russia's attempts to render Kyiv uninhabitable, 72% of the city's residents said in September that they are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology reported in early October. The authorities are striving to maintain normal life in the city, where the curfew has been shortened and now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. Some facilities have even been allowed to continue operating during "yellow" alerts. During "red" alerts, however, people must immediately seek shelter: This could mean ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or massive combined attacks.
